title: BGP Support for Four-Octet Autonomous System (AS) Number Space
summary: Extends BGP so Autonomous System numbers can be carried in four octets instead of two. This expands the supply of AS numbers. It is a standards-track document, replaced by RFC 6793.

eli5.summary: Two-digit house numbers ran out, so this lets networks use longer ones. It makes more numbers available for the networks that make up the Internet.

how do old and new bgp speakers interact
subtitle: Expanding BGP to use 32-bit Autonomous System numbers instead of 16-bit.

tldr.problem: BGP used 16-bit (2-octet) Autonomous System numbers, limiting the address space to 65,535 networks. This limit was approaching exhaustion as the Internet grew.
tldr.mechanism: New BGP speakers advertise support for 4-octet AS numbers via capability negotiation and can encode AS path information using 32-bit AS numbers, while maintaining backward compatibility with older BGP speakers through new optional attributes.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 6793, which refined the specification.

today: RFC 4893 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 6793, which provides refinements to the 4-octet AS number specification.

sections.title: The Need for Larger AS Numbers
sections.content:
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) identifies Autonomous Systems (AS)—large networks or groups of networks under single administrative control—using an Autonomous System number. Originally, these were encoded as 16-bit (2-octet) values, limiting them to the range 0-65535. As the Internet grew and more networks required unique AS numbers, this limit approached exhaustion.

RFC 4893 specifies how BGP can carry 32-bit (4-octet) AS numbers, expanding the available number space to 0-4294967295 (over 4 billion). The expansion was designed to allow gradual transition, with both 2-octet and 4-octet AS numbers coexisting during migration.
sections.eli5: Internet networks need unique ID numbers. The old system had only 65,000 numbers. This RFC lets them use 4 billion numbers instead, so there is room for all networks.

sections.title: Capability Negotiation and New Attributes
sections.content:
A BGP speaker that supports 4-octet AS numbers advertises this capability to its neighbors using BGP Capability Advertisements (defined in RFC 2842). When two peers both advertise the capability, they use 4-octet AS numbers in both the AS_PATH and AGGREGATOR attributes of BGP UPDATE messages.

To preserve AS path information when communicating with older BGP speakers that only understand 2-octet AS numbers, this RFC introduces two new optional transitive attributes: AS4_PATH (attribute type 17) and AS4_AGGREGATOR (attribute type 18). These parallel attributes carry the full 4-octet AS path information alongside the legacy 2-octet attributes.
sections.eli5: New routers tell old routers they can understand bigger numbers. When sending to old routers, new routers send both old-style and new-style numbers so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Mixed Deployments with Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The specification defines three interaction scenarios. When two new BGP speakers peer, they exchange only 4-octet AS numbers, and AS4_PATH and AS4_AGGREGATOR attributes SHOULD NOT be used. When a new speaker peers with an old speaker, the new speaker MUST send 2-octet AS numbers in the regular AS_PATH attribute, but SHOULD also send AS4_PATH containing the 4-octet values.

Non-mappable 4-octet AS numbers (those greater than 65535) are represented as the reserved 2-octet number AS_TRANS (value 23456) in messages to old speakers. This preserves the AS path length property and allows proper path validation. When a new speaker receives updates from an old speaker, it reconstructs the full AS path by combining information from both attributes.
sections.eli5: When two new routers talk, they use the new system. When new talks to old, the new one sends both formats so the old one understands. A special placeholder number fills in for big numbers the old router cannot handle.

sections.title: Transition and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC allows one Autonomous System or one BGP speaker to upgrade at a time, supporting a gradual migration. To simplify transition, an entire Autonomous System must have all its BGP speakers upgraded before that AS can use a 4-octet AS number that is not mappable from 2 octets.

Old BGP speakers MUST NOT use AS_TRANS as their own Autonomous System number. In some complex aggregation scenarios involving multiple old routers in series, it is theoretically possible to lose part of the AS path information when routes are aggregated. However, the RFC notes that when the aggregated route is less specific than its component routes, this loss does not create a routing loop risk.
sections.eli5: Routers can upgrade one at a time. All routers in one network must upgrade together before using the really big numbers. The transition is careful so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Communities and IANA Registry Expansion
sections.content:
BGP Communities attribute uses the high-order 2 octets of a 4-octet value to identify an AS, which does not work for 4-octet AS numbers. The RFC recommends that BGP speakers using 4-octet AS numbers use the Four-octet AS Specific Extended Communities instead of the traditional BGP Communities attribute.

IANA expands the AS number registry from 0-65535 to 0-4294967295, with no changes to existing allocation policies. IANA also assigned BGP Capability code 65 for 4-octet AS number support, and established new BGP attribute type codes: type 17 for AS4_PATH and type 18 for AS4_AGGREGATOR.
sections.eli5: Some BGP features use 2-byte AS numbers internally and need different versions for bigger numbers. IANA set aside official code numbers for all the new pieces.
